concepts.label: Gender Division and the Public/Private Division
concepts.cardText: Gender division is a hierarchical social division. It is seen as natural and unchangeable, but it is based on social expectations and stereotypes, not biology. Boys and girls are brought up to believe women's main responsibility is housework and children, giving a sexual division of labour: women do the work inside the home, men the work outside. When these jobs are paid for, men take them up. Women's work is not valued, and their role in public life, especially politics, is minimal.
concepts.hint: Is the gender division natural, or does it come from how society brings up boys and girls?
concepts.probe: What is the sexual division of labour, and how does it affect women's role in public life?
concepts.causeChain: Social expectations and stereotypes -> sexual division of labour (women inside the home, men outside) -> women's work not valued -> women's role in public life, especially politics, is minimal

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the sexual division of labour to women's minimal role in public life and politics.

keyPoints.text: Gender division is a form of hierarchical social division seen everywhere. It tends to be understood as natural and unchangeable. However, it is not based on biology but on social expectations and stereotypes.
keyPoints.followUp: Is gender division natural, or does it come from somewhere else? Explain.

checks.criterion: States that the gender division is not based on biology but on social expectations and stereotypes.

keyPoints.text: Boys and girls are brought up to believe that the main responsibility of women is housework and bringing up children. This is reflected in a sexual division of labour: women do all work inside the home and men do all the work outside the home. When these jobs are paid for, men are ready to take up these works; most tailors or cooks in hotels are men.
keyPoints.followUp: How is work usually divided between women and men, and what happens when the same work is paid?

requiredEvidence: men do all the work outside
when these jobs are paid for

checks.criterion: Explains the sexual division of labour: women do the work inside the home and men do the work outside the home.
Notes that men are ready to do such work when it is paid for, for example most tailors or cooks in hotels are men.

keyPoints.text: It is not that women do not work outside their home. In villages, women fetch water, collect fuel and work in the fields. The majority of women do some sort of paid work in addition to domestic labour. But their work is not valued and does not get recognition.

requiredEvidence: paid work in addition to domestic labour

checks.criterion: States that women's work, including paid work outside the home, is not valued or recognised.

keyPoints.text: The result of this division of labour is that although women constitute half of the humanity, their role in public life, especially politics, is minimal in most societies.
keyPoints.followUp: What is the result of this division of labour for women's role in public life?

checks.criterion: States that women's role in public life, especially politics, is minimal in most societies.

acceptedExamples: Most tailors or cooks in hotels are men
Women in villages fetch water, collect fuel and work in the fields

misconceptions.fix: The gender division is not based on biology but on social expectations and stereotypes.

concepts.label: Feminist Movements
concepts.cardText: Earlier only men could take part in public affairs, vote and contest elections. Women in many countries organised and agitated for equal rights, including voting rights, a better political and legal status, and educational and career opportunities. More radical women's movements aimed at equality in personal and family life too; these are called feminist movements. This political mobilisation helped improve women's role in public life.
concepts.hint: What did women's movements demand, and what changed because of them?
concepts.probe: What did feminist movements demand, and how did political mobilisation improve women's role in public life?
concepts.causeChain: Women organise and agitate for equal rights -> gender issue raised in politics -> political mobilisation -> women's role in public life improves

causeLinks.criterion: Connects women's political mobilisation and agitation to the improvement in women's role in public life.

keyPoints.text: Women in different parts of the world organised and agitated for equal rights. There were agitations for the extension of voting rights to women. These agitations demanded enhancing the political and legal status of women and improving their educational and career opportunities.
keyPoints.followUp: What did women's agitations around the world demand?

checks.criterion: States that women organised and agitated for equal rights, such as voting rights, better political and legal status, or educational and career opportunities.

keyPoints.text: More radical women's movements aimed at equality in personal and family life as well. These movements are called feminist movements. A feminist is a woman or a man who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men.

requiredEvidence: equality in personal and family life

checks.criterion: Explains feminist movements (equality in personal and family life too) or defines a feminist as a woman or a man who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men.

keyPoints.text: Political expression of gender division and political mobilisation on this question helped to improve women's role in public life. We now find women working as scientists, doctors, engineers, lawyers, managers and college and university teachers. In Scandinavian countries, such as Sweden, Norway and Finland, the participation of women in public life is very high.
keyPoints.followUp: How has political mobilisation changed women's role in public life? Give an example.

requiredEvidence: improve women's role in public life

checks.criterion: States that political mobilisation on gender helped improve women's role in public life (for example women as scientists, doctors, engineers or managers).
Mentions that participation of women in public life is very high in Scandinavian countries such as Sweden, Norway and Finland.

acceptedExamples: Agitations in different countries for the extension of voting rights to women
Sweden, Norway and Finland, where women's participation in public life is very high
Exercise (match): a person who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men is a feminist

misconceptions.fix: A feminist is a woman or a man who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men.

verify.quote: Women in different parts of the world organised and agitated for equal rights.
These movements are called feminist movements.
A woman or a man who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men.
helped to improve women's role in public life

concepts.label: Disadvantages Women Face in India
concepts.cardText: India is still a male-dominated, patriarchal society. The literacy rate among women is 54 per cent against 76 per cent among men, and girls drop out because parents prefer to spend on boys' education. Women are few in highly paid jobs; an average woman works one hour more a day than a man, but much of her work is unpaid and not valued. Despite the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, women are paid less than men. Sex-selective abortion has brought the child sex ratio down to 919, and women face harassment and violence.
concepts.hint: Think of education, work, wages, the child sex ratio and safety.
concepts.probe: In what ways do women in India face disadvantage, discrimination and oppression?
concepts.causeChain: Patriarchal society -> parents prefer to spend on sons' education and prefer sons -> girls drop out; sex-selective abortion -> child sex ratio falls to 919

causeLinks.criterion: Connects parents preferring sons and sex-selective abortion to the decline in the child sex ratio.

keyPoints.text: In our country, women still lag much behind men despite some improvement since Independence. Ours is still a male-dominated, patriarchal society. Patriarchy, literally rule by father, refers to a system that values men more and gives them power over women.

checks.criterion: Describes India as a male-dominated, patriarchal society, or defines patriarchy as a system that values men more and gives them power over women.

keyPoints.text: The literacy rate among women is only 54 per cent compared with 76 per cent among men. A smaller proportion of girl students go for higher studies. Girls perform as well as boys in school, but they drop out because parents prefer to spend their resources for their boys' education.
keyPoints.followUp: How do girls and women compare with boys and men in literacy and higher studies, and why?

checks.criterion: Mentions the gap in literacy (54 per cent among women against 76 per cent among men) or that fewer girls go for higher studies.
Explains that girls drop out because parents prefer to spend their resources on boys' education.

keyPoints.text: The proportion of women among the highly paid and valued jobs is still very small. On an average, an Indian woman works one hour more than an average man every day, yet much of her work is not paid and therefore often not valued. The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 provides that equal wages should be paid to equal work, but in almost all areas of work women are paid less than men.
keyPoints.followUp: How is women's work treated differently from men's work in India?

checks.criterion: Mentions that an average woman works more hours a day than a man (about one hour more), but much of her work is unpaid and not valued.
States that although the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 provides equal wages for equal work, women are paid less than men in almost all areas of work.

keyPoints.text: In many parts of India, parents prefer to have sons and find ways to have the girl child aborted before she is born. Such sex-selective abortion led to a decline in child sex ratio (number of girl children per thousand boys) in the country to merely 919.
keyPoints.followUp: How has the preference for sons affected the number of girls being born?

checks.criterion: Mentions that parents prefer sons and sex-selective abortion takes place.
Mentions the decline in the child sex ratio (girl children per thousand boys) to 919.

keyPoints.text: There are reports of various kinds of harassment, exploitation and violence against women. Urban areas have become particularly unsafe for women. They are not safe even within their own home from beating, harassment and other forms of domestic violence.

checks.criterion: Mentions harassment, exploitation or violence against women, including domestic violence.

acceptedExamples: Time use survey: an average woman works a little over seven and a half hours a day, an average man six and a half hours
Child sex ratio falling below 850 or even 800 in some States (Census 2011)
Exercise: 'Mention different aspects of life in which women are discriminated or disadvantaged in India.'

misconceptions.wrong: Because of the Equal Remuneration Act, women in India are now paid the same as men.
misconceptions.fix: The Act provides that equal wages should be paid for equal work, but in almost all areas of work women are paid less than men, even when both do exactly the same work.

The literacy rate among women is only 54 per cent compared with 76 per cent among men.
an Indian woman works one hour more than an average man every day
The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 provides that equal wages should be paid to equal work.
Such sex-selective abortion led to a decline in child sex ratio
Urban areas have become particularly unsafe for women.
Mention different aspects of life in which women are discriminated or disadvantaged in India.

concepts.label: Women's Political Representation
concepts.cardText: Feminists concluded that unless women control power, their problems will not get adequate attention, so more women are needed as elected representatives. In India, women reached 14.36 per cent of the Lok Sabha only in 2019, and are under 5 per cent in State Assemblies. One-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women, giving more than 10 lakh elected women representatives. The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023 gives 33 per cent reservation in the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly.
concepts.hint: Why do women's movements want more women in legislatures, and what has reservation achieved?
concepts.probe: What is the status of women's representation in India's legislative bodies, and how is it being improved?
concepts.causeChain: Women's issues not given adequate attention -> unless women control power, problems ignored -> demand for more women representatives -> reservation of one-third seats in local bodies, and 33 per cent under the 2023 Act

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the argument that women's problems need women in power to making it legally binding to reserve seats for women.

keyPoints.text: Issues related to women's well being are not given adequate attention. This has led many feminists and women's movements to the conclusion that unless women control power, their problems will not get adequate attention. One way to ensure this is to have more women as elected representatives.
keyPoints.followUp: Why do many women's movements believe that women need to hold power themselves?

checks.criterion: Explains that unless women control power their problems will not get adequate attention, so more women are needed as elected representatives.

keyPoints.text: In India, the proportion of women in legislature has been very low. The percentage of elected women members in Lok Sabha touched 14.36 per cent of its total strength for the first time in 2019. Their share in the state assemblies is less than 5 per cent. India is among the bottom group of nations in the world, and cabinets are largely all-male.
keyPoints.followUp: How well are women represented in India's Lok Sabha and state assemblies?

checks.criterion: States that women's representation in Indian legislatures is very low (for example 14.36 per cent of the Lok Sabha in 2019, under 5 per cent in State Assemblies).

keyPoints.text: One way to solve this problem is to make it legally binding to have a fair proportion of women in the elected bodies. This is what the Panchayati Raj has done in India. One-third of seats in local government bodies, in panchayats and municipalities, are now reserved for women. Now there are more than 10 lakh elected women representatives in rural and urban local bodies.
keyPoints.followUp: What has Panchayati Raj done to increase the number of women in elected bodies?

checks.criterion: States that one-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women.
Mentions that there are more than 10 lakh elected women representatives in rural and urban local bodies.

keyPoints.text: Women's organisations demanded a similar reservation of at least one-third of seats in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies. In 2023, the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (Women's Reservation Act, 2023) was passed, which will give 33 percent reservation of seats for women in Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and also Delhi Assembly.

checks.criterion: Mentions the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (Women's Reservation Act, 2023), giving 33 per cent reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.

keyPoints.text: Gender division is an example that some form of social division needs to be expressed in politics. This also shows that disadvantaged groups do benefit when social divisions become a political issue.

requiredEvidence: needs to be expressed in politics

checks.criterion: Concludes that disadvantaged groups benefit when a social division such as gender becomes a political issue.

acceptedExamples: More than 10 lakh elected women representatives in rural and urban local bodies
Exercise: 'What is the status of women's representation in India's legislative bodies?'
Exercise: 'In India seats are reserved for women in Panchayati Raj bodies' (option d)

misconceptions.wrong: All social divisions, including gender, should be kept out of politics.
misconceptions.fix: Gender division shows that some forms of social division need to be expressed in politics; disadvantaged groups do benefit when social divisions become a political issue.

Their share in the state assemblies is less than 5 per cent.
Now there are more than 10 lakh elected women representatives in rural and urban local bodies.
Adhiniyam (Womens' Reservation Act, 2023) has been passed which will give 33 percent reservation of seats for women
Gender division is an example that some form of social division needs to be expressed in politics.

concepts.label: Religion and Politics
concepts.cardText: Religious differences are often expressed in politics. Gandhiji said religion can never be separated from politics, meaning the moral values that inform all religions. Human rights groups ask the government to protect religious minorities, and the women's movement wants family laws of all religions made more equitable. Ideas drawn from religion can play a role in politics, and the state may regulate religion to prevent discrimination, as long as every religion is treated equally.
concepts.hint: Is every link between religion and politics wrong? What did Gandhiji mean by religion?
concepts.probe: When is the relationship between religion and politics not wrong or dangerous?
concepts.causeChain: Religion is expressed in politics -> acceptable when it brings moral values, protects minorities or makes laws more equitable -> not wrong as long as every religion is treated equally

keyPoints.text: Gandhiji used to say that religion can never be separated from politics. What he meant by religion was not any particular religion like Hinduism or Islam but moral values that inform all religions. He believed that politics must be guided by ethics drawn from religion.
keyPoints.followUp: What did Gandhiji mean when he spoke about religion and politics?

requiredEvidence: moral values that inform all religions

checks.criterion: Explains that by religion Gandhiji meant the moral values that inform all religions, and that politics must be guided by ethics drawn from religion.

keyPoints.text: Human rights groups have demanded that the Government should take special steps to prevent communal riots and protect religious minorities. Women's movement has argued that family laws of all religions discriminate against women and demanded that government change these laws to make them more equitable.

checks.criterion: Mentions human rights groups demanding special steps to prevent communal riots and protect religious minorities.
Mentions the women's movement demanding that family laws of all religions be made more equitable.

keyPoints.text: Ideas, ideals and values drawn from different religions can and perhaps should play a role in politics. People should be able to express in politics their needs, interests and demands as a member of a religious community. These political acts are not wrong as long as they treat every religion equally.
keyPoints.followUp: In what ways can ideas and values from religion play a fair role in politics?

requiredEvidence: can and perhaps should play a role in politics

checks.criterion: States that religion playing a role in politics is not wrong as long as every religion is treated equally.

acceptedExamples: Gandhiji's view that politics must be guided by ethics drawn from religion
Women's movement demanding equitable family laws

misconceptions.wrong: Any link between religion and politics is communal.
misconceptions.fix: Ideas and values drawn from religions can play a role in politics. Such political acts are not wrong as long as they treat every religion equally.

verify.quote: Gandhiji used to say that religion can never be separated from politics.
Women's movement has argued that family laws of all religions discriminate against women.
These political acts are not wrong as long as they treat every religion equally.

concepts.label: Communalism
concepts.cardText: The problem begins when religion is seen as the basis of the nation and is expressed in politics in exclusive and partisan terms: one religion is presented as superior, demands are made against another group, and state power is used to dominate. Communal politics is based on the idea that religion is the principal basis of social community, so followers of one religion are one community with the same interests. In its extreme form, people of different religions cannot live as equal citizens in one nation. This belief is fundamentally flawed: there are many voices inside every community.
concepts.hint: What does communal politics assume about the followers of one religion? Why is that assumption wrong?
concepts.probe: What is communal politics, and why is the belief behind it fundamentally flawed?
concepts.causeChain: Religion treated as the principal basis of social community -> followers seen as one community with the same interests, opposed to others -> in its extreme form, domination or separate nations; but people have many identities -> the belief is fundamentally flawed

causeLinks.criterion: Explains that the communal belief is flawed because people of one religion have many roles and identities and many voices that would be suppressed.

keyPoints.text: The problem begins when religion is seen as the basis of the nation. It becomes more acute when religion is expressed in politics in exclusive and partisan terms: when beliefs of one religion are presented as superior, when the demands of one religious group are formed in opposition to another and when state power is used to establish domination of one religious group over the rest. This manner of using religion in politics is communal politics.
keyPoints.followUp: When does the link between religion and politics become a problem?

checks.criterion: Explains communal politics as using religion in politics in exclusive and partisan terms: one religion presented as superior, demands made in opposition to another group, or state power used to dominate.

keyPoints.text: Communal politics is based on the idea that religion is the principal basis of social community. The followers of a particular religion must belong to one community and their fundamental interests are the same. People who follow different religions cannot belong to the same social community. In its extreme form, communalism leads to the belief that people belonging to different religions cannot live as equal citizens within one nation.
keyPoints.followUp: What does communal politics assume about the followers of a religion?

checks.criterion: States that communal politics treats religion as the principal basis of social community, so the followers of one religion are one community with the same interests.
Mentions that in its extreme form, communalism holds that people of different religions cannot live as equal citizens in one nation.

keyPoints.text: This belief is fundamentally flawed. People of one religion do not have the same interests and aspirations in every context. Everyone has several other roles, positions and identities. There are many voices inside every community, and any attempt to bring all followers of one religion together in context other than religion is bound to suppress many voices within that community.
keyPoints.followUp: Why is the belief that all followers of a religion share the same interests wrong?

checks.criterion: Explains that the communal belief is flawed because people of one religion have different interests, roles and identities, and there are many voices inside every community.

acceptedExamples: Exercise: communal politics is based on the beliefs that one religion is superior to others and that followers of a particular religion constitute one community (option c: A and C)
Exercise (match): a person who says that religion is the principal basis of community is a communalist

misconceptions.wrong: People who follow the same religion all have the same interests.
misconceptions.fix: People of one religion do not have the same interests and aspirations in every context. Everyone has several other roles, positions and identities.

verify.quote: The problem begins when religion is seen as the basis of the nation.
This manner of using religion in politics is communal politics.
Communal politics is based on the idea that religion is the principal basis of social community.
This belief is fundamentally flawed.
There are many voices inside every community.

concepts.label: Forms of Communalism
concepts.cardText: Communalism takes several forms: everyday beliefs (religious prejudices, stereotypes and belief in the superiority of one's religion); a quest for political dominance (majoritarian dominance for the majority, or a separate political unit for a minority); political mobilisation on religious lines using sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeal and plain fear; and, in its ugliest form, communal violence, riots and massacres, as at the time of Partition.
concepts.hint: Think of four forms: everyday beliefs, dominance, mobilisation and violence.
concepts.probe: What are the different forms that communalism can take in politics? Give an example of each.
concepts.causeChain: Communal mind -> everyday prejudice and stereotypes -> quest for political dominance -> mobilisation on religious lines -> in its ugliest form, communal violence

keyPoints.text: The most common expression of communalism is in everyday beliefs. These routinely involve religious prejudices, stereotypes of religious communities and belief in the superiority of one's religion over other religions.

checks.criterion: Names everyday beliefs (religious prejudices, stereotypes or belief in one's religion's superiority) as a form of communalism.

keyPoints.text: A communal mind often leads to a quest for political dominance of one's own religious community. For those belonging to majority community, this takes the form of majoritarian dominance. For those belonging to the minority community, it can take the form of a desire to form a separate political unit.
keyPoints.followUp: What kind of political goal does a communal mind often lead to, for majority and for minority communities?

checks.criterion: Names the quest for political dominance as a form of communalism: majoritarian dominance for a majority, or a separate political unit for a minority.

keyPoints.text: Political mobilisation on religious lines is another frequent form of communalism. This involves the use of sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeal and plain fear in order to bring the followers of one religion together in the political arena. In electoral politics, this often involves special appeal to the interests or emotions of voters of one religion in preference to others.
keyPoints.followUp: How do some leaders use religion to bring people together for political purposes?

checks.criterion: Names political mobilisation on religious lines (sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeal or fear) as a form of communalism.

keyPoints.text: Sometimes communalism takes its most ugly form of communal violence, riots and massacre. India and Pakistan suffered some of the worst communal riots at the time of the Partition. The post-Independence period has also seen large scale communal violence.

checks.criterion: Names communal violence, riots and massacres (for example at the time of Partition) as the ugliest form of communalism.

acceptedExamples: Communal riots in India and Pakistan at the time of Partition
Special appeal to voters of one religion in electoral politics
Exercise: 'State different forms of communal politics with one example each.'

misconceptions.wrong: Only a majority community can be communal.
misconceptions.fix: For a majority community communalism takes the form of majoritarian dominance; for a minority community it can take the form of a desire to form a separate political unit.

verify.quote: The most common expression of communalism is in everyday beliefs.
For those belonging to majority community, this takes the form of majoritarian dominance.
Political mobilisation on religious lines is another frequent form of communalism.
India and Pakistan suffered some of the worst communal riots at the time of the Partition.
State different forms of communal politics with one example each.

concepts.label: Secular State
concepts.cardText: The makers of our Constitution chose the model of a secular state. There is no official religion for the Indian state, unlike Buddhism in Sri Lanka, Islam in Pakistan and Christianity in England. The Constitution gives everyone freedom to profess, practice and propagate any religion, or none; it prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion; and it allows the state to intervene in religion to ensure equality within religious communities, for example by banning untouchability. A secular Constitution is necessary but not sufficient to combat communalism.
concepts.hint: Does the Indian state have an official religion? What may the state do in matters of religion?
concepts.probe: Which constitutional provisions make India a secular state, and why is a secular Constitution not enough by itself?
concepts.causeChain: Communalism is a major challenge to democracy -> makers of the Constitution chose a secular state -> no official religion, freedom of religion, no discrimination, state may intervene for equality -> still, prejudice and religion-based mobilisation must be countered in everyday life and politics

causeLinks.criterion: Connects communalism being a major challenge to democracy to the Constitution's choice of a secular state.

keyPoints.text: Communalism was and continues to be one of the major challenges to democracy in our country. The makers of our Constitution were aware of this challenge. That is why they chose the model of a secular state.

checks.criterion: States that because communalism is a major challenge to democracy, the makers of the Constitution chose a secular state.

keyPoints.text: There is no official religion for the Indian state. Unlike the status of Buddhism in Sri Lanka, that of Islam in Pakistan and that of Christianity in England, our Constitution does not give a special status to any religion.
keyPoints.followUp: Does the Indian state follow any religion? How is India different from some other countries here?

checks.criterion: States that the Indian state has no official religion and the Constitution gives no special status to any religion.

keyPoints.text: The Constitution provides to all individuals and communities freedom to profess, practice and propagate any religion, or not to follow any. The Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion.
keyPoints.followUp: What freedoms and protections does the Constitution give about religion?

requiredEvidence: freedom to profess, practice and propagate
prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion

checks.criterion: Mentions the freedom to profess, practice and propagate any religion, or not to follow any.
Mentions that the Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion.

keyPoints.text: At the same time, the Constitution allows the state to intervene in the matters of religion in order to ensure equality within religious communities. For example, it bans untouchability.

requiredEvidence: intervene in the matters of religion

checks.criterion: States that the Constitution allows the state to intervene in religion to ensure equality within religious communities, for example by banning untouchability.

keyPoints.text: Secularism constitutes one of the foundations of our country. Communalism threatens the very idea of India. A secular Constitution like ours is necessary but not sufficient to combat communalism. Communal prejudices and propaganda need to be countered in everyday life and religion-based mobilisation needs to be countered in the arena of politics.
keyPoints.followUp: Is a secular Constitution enough to stop communalism? What else is needed?

checks.criterion: States that a secular Constitution is necessary but not sufficient; communal prejudice must be countered in everyday life and religion-based mobilisation in politics.

acceptedExamples: Buddhism in Sri Lanka, Islam in Pakistan and Christianity in England as official religions, unlike India
The constitutional ban on untouchability

Exercise: the statement that India's Constitution 'gives official status to one religion' is wrong (option b)

misconceptions.wrong: A secular state means the state has nothing to do with religion at all.
misconceptions.fix: India has no official religion, but the Constitution allows the state to intervene in matters of religion to ensure equality within religious communities, for example by banning untouchability.

concepts.label: Caste Inequalities
concepts.cardText: Unlike gender and religion, caste division is special to India. In the caste system, hereditary occupational division was sanctioned by rituals; members of a caste practised similar occupations, married within the group and did not eat with other castes. The system was based on exclusion of and discrimination against 'outcaste' groups through untouchability. Reformers like Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker worked against it. With economic development, urbanisation, education, occupational mobility and the weakening of landlords, the old notions of caste hierarchy are breaking down.
concepts.hint: What made the caste system different from other divisions of labour? What has weakened it?
concepts.probe: What was special about the caste system, and which changes have weakened the old caste hierarchy?
concepts.causeChain: Economic development, urbanisation, literacy and education, occupational mobility, weakening of landlords (plus reformers' efforts) -> old notions of caste hierarchy break down

causeLinks.criterion: Connects socio-economic changes such as urbanisation, education and occupational mobility to the breaking down of old notions of caste hierarchy.

keyPoints.text: Unlike gender and religion, caste division is special to India. In most societies occupations are passed on from one generation to another; the caste system is an extreme form of this, in which hereditary occupational division was sanctioned by rituals. Members of the same caste practised the same or similar occupation, married within the caste group and did not eat with members from other caste groups.
keyPoints.followUp: What makes caste division different from other social divisions, and how did the caste system work?

checks.criterion: States that caste division is special to India and that hereditary occupational division was sanctioned by rituals.
Mentions that caste members practised similar occupations, married within the caste group or did not eat with other castes.

keyPoints.text: Caste system was based on exclusion of and discrimination against the 'outcaste' groups, who were subjected to the inhuman practice of untouchability. Political leaders and social reformers like Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker worked to establish a society in which caste inequalities are absent.

checks.criterion: Mentions exclusion of and discrimination against 'outcaste' groups through untouchability.
Names reformers who worked against caste inequality, such as Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar or Periyar Ramaswami Naicker.

keyPoints.text: With economic development, large scale urbanisation, growth of literacy and education, occupational mobility and the weakening of the position of landlords in the villages, the old notions of caste hierarchy are breaking down. In urban areas it does not matter much who is walking along next to us on a street or eating at the next table in a restaurant. The Constitution of India prohibited any caste-based discrimination.
keyPoints.followUp: Which changes in society have weakened the old caste hierarchy?

checks.criterion: Names socio-economic changes such as economic development, urbanisation, literacy and education, occupational mobility or the weakening of landlords.
States that the old notions of caste hierarchy are breaking down.

acceptedExamples: In urban areas, it does not matter much who is eating at the next table in a restaurant
Exercise: 'Social divisions based on caste are peculiar to India.'
Census 2011: Scheduled Castes 16.6 per cent and Scheduled Tribes 8.6 per cent of the population

concepts.label: Caste Has Not Disappeared
concepts.cardText: Caste has not disappeared from contemporary India. Most people still marry within their own caste or tribe, and untouchability has not ended completely. Effects of centuries of advantages and disadvantages continue: groups that had access to education did well in modern education too, so 'upper castes' are disproportionately present in the urban middle classes. Caste is still closely linked to economic status: average economic status follows the old hierarchy, extreme poverty is much higher for the lowest castes, and upper castes are over-represented among the rich.
concepts.hint: Which old aspects of caste persist, and how is caste still linked to economic status?
concepts.probe: How do caste inequalities still continue in India?
concepts.causeChain: Centuries of unequal access to education and resources -> groups with access did well in modern education, others lagged -> 'upper castes' over-represented in urban middle classes -> caste still linked to economic status

causeLinks.criterion: Connects centuries of accumulated advantages and disadvantages (such as access to education) to caste still being linked to economic status today.

keyPoints.text: Caste has not disappeared from contemporary India. Some of the older aspects of caste have persisted. Even now most people marry within their own caste or tribe. Untouchability has not ended completely, despite constitutional prohibition.
keyPoints.followUp: Which older practices of caste still continue in India today?

checks.criterion: States that caste persists: most people still marry within their own caste or tribe, or untouchability has not ended completely.

keyPoints.text: Effects of centuries of advantages and disadvantages continue to be felt today. The caste groups that had access to education under the old system have done very well in acquiring modern education as well, while those that did not have access have naturally lagged behind. That is why there is a disproportionately large presence of 'upper caste' among the urban middle classes. Caste continues to be closely linked to economic status.
keyPoints.followUp: How do past advantages and disadvantages of castes still affect people today?

checks.criterion: Explains that effects of centuries of advantages and disadvantages continue, for example groups with past access to education did well in modern education.
States that caste continues to be closely linked to economic status.

keyPoints.text: National Sample Survey evidence shows that the average economic status of caste groups still follows the old hierarchy: the 'upper' castes are best off and the Dalits and Adivasis are worst off. The proportion living in extreme poverty is much higher for the lowest castes, and the upper castes are heavily over-represented among the rich.

checks.criterion: Mentions evidence that economic status follows the old caste hierarchy, that extreme poverty is higher among the lowest castes, or that upper castes are over-represented among the rich.

acceptedExamples: NSSO 1999-2000: 45.8 per cent of rural Scheduled Tribes and 35.9 per cent of rural Scheduled Castes below the poverty line, against 11.7 per cent of rural Hindu upper castes
Exercise: 'State how caste inequalities are still continuing in India.'

misconceptions.wrong: Caste no longer matters in modern India.
misconceptions.fix: Caste has not disappeared from contemporary India: most people still marry within their own caste or tribe, untouchability has not ended completely, and caste is closely linked to economic status.

Caste continues to be closely linked to economic status.
the upper castes are heavily over-represented among the rich while the lower castes are severely under-represented

concepts.label: Caste in Politics
concepts.cardText: Like communalism, casteism is rooted in the belief that caste is the sole basis of social community, a belief not borne out by experience. Caste takes several forms in politics: parties choose candidates keeping in mind the caste composition of the electorate, and governments include representatives of different castes; parties appeal to caste sentiment, and some are seen as representing certain castes; and universal adult franchise made leaders mobilise political support, bringing new consciousness to castes that were treated as inferior.
concepts.hint: How do parties use caste when choosing candidates and forming governments?
concepts.probe: What forms does caste take in politics?
concepts.causeChain: Universal adult franchise and one-person-one-vote -> leaders must mobilise political support -> parties nominate candidates and appeal to caste sentiment -> new consciousness among castes treated as inferior

causeLinks.criterion: Connects universal adult franchise and one-person-one-vote to political leaders mobilising support along caste lines.

keyPoints.text: As in the case of communalism, casteism is rooted in the belief that caste is the sole basis of social community. According to this way of thinking, people of the same caste belong to a natural social community and have the same interests. Such a belief is not borne out by our experience: caste is one aspect of our experience but it is not the only relevant or the most important aspect.
keyPoints.followUp: What belief about caste lies behind casteism, and does experience support it?

requiredEvidence: not borne out by our experience

checks.criterion: Defines casteism as the belief that caste is the sole basis of social community, and notes that this belief is not borne out by experience.

keyPoints.text: When parties choose candidates in elections, they keep in mind the caste composition of the electorate and nominate candidates from different castes. When governments are formed, political parties usually take care that representatives of different castes and tribes find a place in it. Parties and candidates make appeals to caste sentiment, and some political parties are known to favour some castes.
keyPoints.followUp: How do political parties take caste into account when choosing candidates and forming governments?

checks.criterion: Explains that parties choose candidates keeping in mind the caste composition of the electorate, include different castes in governments, or appeal to caste sentiment.

keyPoints.text: Universal adult franchise and the principle of one-person-one-vote compelled political leaders to gear up to the task of mobilising and securing political support. It also brought new consciousness among the people of castes that were hitherto treated as inferior and low.

checks.criterion: Mentions that universal adult franchise made leaders mobilise political support and brought new consciousness among castes treated as inferior.

acceptedExamples: Parties nominating candidates from different castes to muster support
Exercise (match): a person who thinks that caste is the principal basis of community is a casteist

verify.quote: casteism is rooted in the belief that caste is the sole basis of social community
they keep in mind the caste composition of the electorate
It also brought new consciousness among the people of castes that were hitherto treated as inferior and low.

concepts.label: Elections Are Not All About Caste
concepts.cardText: Elections are not all about caste. No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one caste, so every candidate needs support from more than one caste. No party wins all the votes of a caste; a 'vote bank' only means a large proportion of a caste votes for a party. Many parties may field candidates from the same caste, and ruling parties and sitting MPs and MLAs frequently lose. Party attachment, economic interests and people's assessment of the government's performance also matter.
concepts.hint: Can a candidate win with the votes of one caste alone? What else do voters consider?
concepts.probe: Why can caste alone not determine election results in India?
concepts.causeChain: No constituency has a clear majority of one caste + no party wins all of a caste's votes -> candidates need support from many communities -> other factors (party attachment, economic interests, government performance) also decide elections

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the fact that no constituency has a clear majority of one caste to candidates needing wider support, so factors other than caste decide elections.

keyPoints.text: No parliamentary constituency in the country has a clear majority of one single caste. So, every candidate and party needs to win the confidence of more than one caste and community to win elections.
keyPoints.followUp: Why can no candidate win an election with the support of just one caste?

requiredEvidence: clear majority of one single caste

checks.criterion: States that no parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one caste, so candidates need support from more than one caste and community.

keyPoints.text: No party wins the votes of all the voters of a caste or community. When people say that a caste is a 'vote bank' of one party, it usually means that a large proportion of the voters from that caste vote for that party. Many parties may put up candidates from the same caste, and the ruling party and the sitting MP or MLA frequently lose elections.
keyPoints.followUp: When people say a caste 'belongs' to one party, is that really true? Explain.

checks.criterion: Explains that no party wins all the votes of a caste; a 'vote bank' only means a large proportion of that caste votes for a party.
Mentions that ruling parties and sitting MPs or MLAs frequently lose, which could not happen if castes were frozen in their political preferences.
Mentions that many parties may put up candidates from the same caste.

keyPoints.text: While caste matters in electoral politics, so do many other factors. The voters have strong attachment to political parties which is often stronger than their attachment to their caste. People within the same caste have different interests depending on their economic condition. People's assessment of the performance of the government and the popularity rating of the leaders matter and are often decisive in elections.
keyPoints.followUp: Apart from caste, what else influences how people vote?

checks.criterion: Names other factors that decide elections, such as attachment to parties, economic interests, or people's assessment of the government's performance and of leaders.

acceptedExamples: The ruling party and the sitting MP or MLA frequently losing elections
Exercise: 'State two reasons to say that caste alone cannot determine election results in India.'

misconceptions.wrong: A candidate whose caste is the largest in the constituency will automatically win.
misconceptions.fix: No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste, and no party wins all the votes of a caste. Candidates must win the confidence of more than one caste and community.

verify.quote: No parliamentary constituency in the country has a clear majority of one single caste.
No party wins the votes of all the voters of a caste or community.
Clearly, while caste matters in electoral politics, so do many other factors.
State two reasons to say that caste alone cannot determine election results in India.

concepts.label: Politics in Caste
concepts.cardText: Politics also influences caste: it is not politics that gets caste-ridden, it is caste that gets politicised. Caste groups try to become bigger by incorporating neighbouring castes, enter into coalitions and negotiation with other castes, and new groups such as 'backward' and 'forward' castes appear. Caste politics has given disadvantaged communities, such as Dalits and OBCs, better access to decision making. But politics based on caste alone can divert attention from poverty, development and corruption, and can lead to tension, conflict and violence.
concepts.hint: How does politics change caste groups? Is caste in politics only good or only bad?
concepts.probe: How does caste get politicised, and what are the positive and negative effects of caste in politics?
concepts.causeChain: Politics brings caste into the political arena -> castes expand, form coalitions, new 'backward'/'forward' groups -> disadvantaged groups gain access to decision making; but exclusive focus on caste diverts attention and can cause conflict

causeLinks.criterion: Connects caste being politicised to disadvantaged communities such as Dalits and OBCs gaining space to demand their share of power.

keyPoints.text: Politics too influences the caste system and caste identities by bringing them into the political arena. Thus, it is not politics that gets caste-ridden, it is the caste that gets politicised. Each caste group tries to become bigger by incorporating neighbouring castes or sub-castes; various caste groups enter into a coalition with other castes and thus into dialogue and negotiation; and new kinds of caste groups have come up like 'backward' and 'forward' caste groups.
keyPoints.followUp: How does politics change caste groups, rather than caste changing politics?

checks.criterion: States that it is caste that gets politicised, for example caste groups grow by incorporating sub-castes, form coalitions with other castes, or new 'backward' and 'forward' groups emerge.

keyPoints.text: In some situations, expression of caste differences in politics gives many disadvantaged communities the space to demand their share of power. In this sense, caste politics has helped people from Dalits and OBC castes to gain better access to decision making.
keyPoints.followUp: How has caste politics helped some communities?

checks.criterion: States that caste politics gives disadvantaged communities space to demand their share of power, helping Dalits and OBCs gain better access to decision making.

keyPoints.text: At the same time, exclusive attention to caste can produce negative results. Politics based on caste identity alone is not very healthy in a democracy. It can divert attention from other pressing issues like poverty, development and corruption. In some cases, caste division leads to tensions, conflict and even violence.
keyPoints.followUp: What can go wrong when politics focuses only on caste?

checks.criterion: States that politics based on caste alone can divert attention from issues like poverty, development and corruption, or lead to tension, conflict and violence.

acceptedExamples: New caste groupings such as 'backward' and 'forward' castes in the political arena
Dalits and OBCs gaining better access to decision making

misconceptions.wrong: Caste in politics is always harmful.
misconceptions.fix: Caste plays different roles: it has given disadvantaged communities such as Dalits and OBCs better access to decision making, although politics based on caste alone is not healthy in a democracy.

caste politics has helped people from Dalits and OBC castes to gain better access to decision making
It can divert attention from other pressing issues like poverty, development and corruption.
